title: Bhai Randhir Singh
hook: a revolutionary and devotee whose followers founded the Akhand Kirtani Jatha

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rehat Maryada: a code, agreed. Today, a man who kept his own code inside a prison.

A guard's footsteps go down a stone corridor at night, past an iron door, and fade. From behind the door comes a voice singing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib, steady and unhurried, as if the room were a gurdwara. The guards have heard it before; they'll hear it again tomorrow. The man singing has been sentenced for plotting against the British government, with many years still to serve. The singing doesn't stop.
screen: `FOOTSTEPS IN A STONE CORRIDOR.` → `A VOICE SINGING SHABADS.` → `THE SINGING DOES NOT STOP.`

segments.voice: Bhai Randhir Singh came from the village of Narangwal in Punjab. He was drawn into the Ghadar plans against British rule that came up earlier in this block, and was arrested and given a long prison sentence. He was a revolutionary. He was also, before and after, a man of deep devotion. In jail he was expected to eat what he was given and live as the jail decided. He held to his own strict discipline as a Khalsa Sikh, including about the food he would accept, and when it was refused he went without, for long stretches. His own account of these years, his Jail Letters, describes the hunger, the punishments and the stubbornness in plain terms. Through all of it he kept up kirtan, singing the Gurus' hymns, alone or with any Sikh prisoner who would join him. At Ang 1075 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says that in this dark age, kirtan, singing the Lord's praise, is supreme. After his release, those who gathered around Bhai Randhir Singh formed the Akhand Kirtani Jatha, known for kirtan that can go on through the whole night, and for a strict rehat of their own. Some Sikhs follow that path closely; others admire it from a distance. Either way, it began in a cell, with one voice that wouldn't stop singing.
screen: `REVOLUTIONARY AND DEVOTEE.` · `HE KEPT HIS REHAT IN JAIL.` · `HE KEPT SINGING.` · `KIRTAN THROUGH THE NIGHT.` · then, large: `KIRTAN IN PRISON.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something hard you're carrying right now, then let a song come that steadies you: a shabad, a hymn, a lullaby, anything. Hum it quietly or hear it inside, line by line, while the hard thing sits beside you. If you pray, let Waheguru be the song.
Jail Letters, Bhai Randhir Singh's own account of the hunger, the punishments and the kirtan that carried him through long years in prison.
Your line: kirtan in prison. A song can hold a person up when little else can. Rest well.

howItsDone: The Akhand Kirtani Jatha holds kirtan programs, including all-night kirtan, and its members keep a strict rehat; Bhai Randhir Singh's writings, including his prison letters, are read among his followers and others.
